question: What is DNS resolution doing at a basic level, and where does a sinkhole/proxy like this one sit in that flow?
answer_hinglish:
DNS resolution matlab ek human-readable naam (jaise news.example.com) ko ek IP address mein convert karna, taaki browser us IP par connection bana sake. Normally client (browser/OS) apna configured DNS server se poochta hai, woh server jawab deta hai ya kisi aur server se poochta hai.

Yeh project ek PROXY hai, resolver nahi -- matlab yeh naya naam-se-IP translation khud nahi karta. Client ka query pehle yahan aata hai; agar naam blocklisted hai toh yeh khud jawab de deta hai (bina kisi se poochhe), warna query ko ek configured upstream resolver (jaise 1.1.1.1) ko forward kar deta hai aur uska jawab wapas relay kar deta hai.

is_this_project context ke saath: SinkholeServer ek UDP port (default 15353) par client ke query sunta hai, SinkholeProxy.handle() decide karta hai block/cache/forward, aur agar forward karna hai toh transport.ts upstream se baat karta hai. End result client ke liye bilkul normal DNS jaisa dikhta hai, sirf kuch domains silently gayab ho jaate hain.
why_needed: Interviewer yeh basic mental model check karta hai ki candidate resolution, proxying, aur caching ke beech farak samajhta hai -- yeh poori project ki foundation hai.
real_world_analogy: Socho ek office receptionist hai (yeh proxy) jiske paas ek chhoti 'blacklist' hai -- kuch naam sunke woh seedha 'yeh yahan nahi milega' bol deti hai, baaki ke liye andar jaake asli directory (upstream) se poochkar wapas aati hai.
how_it_works: Query UDP packet ke roop mein aata hai, proxy usse decode karta hai, decision leta hai, aur ek response buffer wapas bhejta hai -- yeh sab server.ts aur proxy.ts mein hota hai.
in_this_project: src/server.ts ka SinkholeServer.listen() UDP socket bind karta hai aur har message proxy.handle() ko de deta hai; demo.ts ka main() isi flow ko end to end dikhata hai -- block, forward, cache hit, sab ek hi run mein.
advantages: Client ko kuch alag setup nahi karna, bas DNS server address badalna hai
Blocking/caching ek central jagah hoti hai, har app mein alag se nahi
disadvantages: Yeh proxy khud resolve nahi karta, isliye upstream down ho toh sab kuch ruk jaata hai
Ek single point jahan se saari queries guzarti hain
common_mistakes: Proxy aur resolver ko same samajh lena
Sochna ki blocklist hit hone par bhi upstream ko call lagta hai
follow_up_questions: Agar upstream khud down ho jaaye toh client ko kya milega?

question: Why does DNS normally use UDP, and when does this project fall back to TCP?
answer_hinglish:
DNS zyadatar UDP par chalta hai kyunki queries chhoti hoti hain aur UDP mein connection setup ka overhead nahi hota -- fire-and-forget, fast. Lekin UDP packets ki ek practical size limit hoti hai; agar jawab bada ho (zyada answers ya bada rdata), toh woh truncate ho sakta hai.

Jab aisa hota hai, server reply ke header mein TC (truncated) bit set kar deta hai. Client/proxy ko yeh dekh kar samajhna padta hai ki 'yeh adhoora jawab hai, same query TCP par phir se bhejo' -- TCP reliable, stream-based hai, size limit practically nahi hai, isliye full answer mil jaata hai.

Is project mein yeh logic UPSTREAM side par hai: transport.ts ka forwardQuery() pehle UDP try karta hai (queryUdp), reply ka TC bit decodeHeader se check karta hai, aur agar tc true hai toh SAME query ko queryTcp() se retry karta hai. Downstream (client-facing) side TCP support NAHI hai -- yeh proxy clients se sirf UDP leta hai, kyunki ad-block jawab hamesha chhote hote hain (ek A record ya empty NXDOMAIN).
why_needed: TC bit samajhna zaroori hai warna ek bada ya incomplete answer silently relay ho sakta hai, jo galat DNS behavior hota.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek postcard (UDP) par itna message nahi likh sakte -- agar zyada likhna hai toh ek poora lifafa (TCP) bhejna padta hai, aur postcard par bata diya jaata hai 'poora message lifafe mein hai'.
how_it_works: decodeHeader() se tc flag padha jaata hai; true hone par queryTcp() SAME raw query bytes ko length-prefixed TCP frame mein bhejta hai (frameTcp), aur full reply read karta hai.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts ka forwardQuery(): `if (!header.tc) return udpReply; return queryTcp(to, query, opts.tcpTimeoutMs);` -- yeh exactly yeh decision hai.
advantages: UDP fast hota hai zyadatar (chhoti) queries ke liye
TCP fallback sirf tab lagta hai jab zaroorat ho, har query par overhead nahi
disadvantages: TCP retry ek extra round trip hai, latency badhati hai bade answers ke liye
Downstream TCP na hone se bade client-facing answers truncate ho sakte, par yahan answers hamesha chhote hain
common_mistakes: TC bit ko error samajh lena, jab woh sirf 'incomplete, TCP try karo' ka signal hai
Same query dobara na bhejna, ek alag query bana dena TCP retry mein
follow_up_questions: Agar client khud se TCP par query bhej de, yeh proxy kya karega?
TCP retry mein connection drop ho jaaye toh kya hota hai?
EDNS(0) UDP size limit badhata hai -- yeh project usse support karta hai?

question: What does a TTL in a DNS answer mean, and why does caching have to respect it?
answer_hinglish:
TTL (time to live) ek number hai seconds mein, jo har answer record ke saath aata hai aur batata hai ki yeh jawab kitni der tak 'valid/fresh' maana jaa sakta hai bina dobara pooche. Jaise 300-second TTL matlab agle 5 minute tak koi bhi isi naam ko poochhe toh same jawab de sakte ho, upstream ko dobara disturb kiye bina.

Caching ko TTL respect karna PADTA hai kyunki real world mein IP addresses badalte rehte hain (server migrate, load balancer change, etc.) -- agar hum TTL ignore karke hamesha purana jawab dete rahen, client galat/outdated server se connect karne ki koshish karega. TTL expire hone ke baad cache ko woh entry 'stale' maan kar drop karna chahiye aur fresh jawab upstream se lena chahiye.

Is project mein ResponseCache.put() ek entry ko `expiresAt = now + ttlSeconds*1000` ke saath store karta hai, aur get() check karta hai ki abhi expire hua ya nahi -- expire ho gaya toh miss treat hota hai aur entry delete ho jaati hai, bilkul jaise asli resolver ka cache karta hai.
why_needed: TTL hi caching aur staleness ke beech ka contract hai -- isse galat samjhna production mein stale/wrong answers dega.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek doodh ke packet par expiry date likhi hoti hai -- jab tak date nahi aayi tab tak use kar sakte ho bina dobara dukaan jaaye, date ke baad fenk dena padta hai.
how_it_works: put() clock.now() + ttlSeconds*1000 ko expiresAt mein store karta hai; get() current time ko expiresAt se compare karta hai.
in_this_project: src/cache.ts ResponseCache.put aur get; TTL `parsed.answers` mein se SMALLEST TTL use hota hai (proxy.ts: `Math.min(...parsed.answers.map(a => a.ttl))`), kyunki pura reply ek hi expiry rakhta hai.
advantages: Upstream par load kam hota hai jab tak answer fresh hai
TTL respect karna client ko correct, non-stale answers deta hai
disadvantages: Chhoti TTL wale naam (jaise load-balanced CDNs) ke liye caching ka benefit kam milta hai
Bahut badi TTL cache karne par ek stale entry zyada der tak reh sakti hai
common_mistakes: Sabse badi TTL use karna jab multiple answers ho, jab sabse CHHOTI use honi chahiye
TTL ko cache hit ke waqt nahi, store ke waqt hi fix maan lena (countdown bhool jaana)
follow_up_questions: Agar ek answer mein multiple A records ho, alag TTLs ke saath, kaunsi use hogi?
TTL = 0 ka kya matlab hai -- cache karna chahiye ya nahi?
Negative caching (NXDOMAIN ke liye TTL) kaise kaam karta, real DNS mein?

question: What does a blocklist/sinkhole actually do to a DNS query for a blocked domain?
answer_hinglish:
Ek blocklist/sinkhole ek blocked domain ke query ko UPSTREAM tak jaane hi NAHI deta -- proxy khud, apni taraf se, ek jawab bana kar de deta hai, jaise asli resolver ne diya ho. Yeh resolution ko 'rok' deta hai: client ko koi real IP nahi milta jahan woh ad/tracker server tak pahunch sake.

Do tareeke se yeh kiya ja sakta hai: ek, NXDOMAIN bol dena ('yeh naam exist hi nahi karta'); do, ek 'sinkhole' IP (jaise 0.0.0.0) de dena jaise woh naam resolve ho gaya ho par kisi useless jagah. Dono mein client ko tracker server ka REAL IP kabhi nahi milta.

Is project mein yeh check SinkholeProxy.handle() mein hota hai -- `this.blockList.isBlocked(name)` true aane par, upstream ko CONTACT kiye bina hi buildBlockResponse() call ho jaata hai aur stats.blocked badhta hai. Yeh pura kaam ek local trie lookup hai, koi network call nahi lagti, isliye blocked queries sabse FAST path hain is proxy mein.
why_needed: Blocking ka pura point hi yeh hai ki client kabhi tracker se network-level connect na kar sake -- browser-level ad blockers ke bajaye yeh network ki jad se rok deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek security guard entry gate par hi ek naam dekh kar bol de 'yahan koi aisa office nahi hai', bina andar jaake directory check kiye.
how_it_works: isBlocked() ek trie walk hai; true milne par proxy khud hi ek response encode kar deta hai, upstream.ts ya transport.ts ko kabhi call nahi lagti.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts handle(): `if (this.blockList.isBlocked(name)) { this.stats.blocked++; return this.buildBlockResponse(base, q); }` -- yeh check cache lookup aur forward se PEHLE hota hai.
advantages: Blocked query kabhi upstream tak nahi jaati -- network-level privacy/speed benefit
Local trie lookup fast hai, latency add nahi karta
disadvantages: Blocklist khud maintain karni padti hai, outdated ho sakti hai
Overblocking ka risk -- agar galat domain list mein chala jaaye toh legit site bhi block ho jaati
common_mistakes: Sochna ki blocking cache ke BAAD check hoti hai, jab asal mein cache check se pehle hoti hai
Block hone par bhi upstream ko call lagne ki galat dhaarna
follow_up_questions: Blocked query bhi stats mein count hoti hai -- kyun zaroori hai yeh?
Agar blocklist khaali ho, kya proxy ka behavior badal jaata hai?
Allowlist/exception kaise add karoge is design mein?

question: What is the difference between NXDOMAIN and a normal (NOERROR) DNS answer?
answer_hinglish:
NOERROR matlab query successfully process hui aur (kam se kam ek) answer record mila -- naam exist karta hai aur resolve ho gaya. NXDOMAIN ek rcode hai jo kehta hai 'yeh naam exist hi NAHI karta' -- koi record nahi milega, kyunki naam galat hai ya register nahi hai.

Yeh dono alag hain SERVFAIL se bhi: SERVFAIL kehta hai 'main is query ko process nahi kar paya' (timeout, error, kuch gadbad) -- naam exist karta hoga ya nahi, pata nahi chala. NXDOMAIN ek definitive 'no' hai, SERVFAIL ek 'maine try hi nahi kiya properly' hai.

Is project mein dono use hote hain: block mode 'nxdomain' mein blocked domain ko NXDOMAIN milta hai (RCODE.NXDOMAIN); jab block mode 'sinkhole' hai aur query type A hai, tab NOERROR ke saath ek fake A record milta hai; aur jab upstream fail ho jaaye, tab SERVFAIL. Teeno ek alag rcode byte hain (`RCODE = { NOERROR: 0, FORMERR: 1, SERVFAIL: 2, NXDOMAIN: 3, NOTIMP: 4, REFUSED: 5 }`), jo har response header mein encode hote hain.
why_needed: Interview mein rcode confusion common hai -- NXDOMAIN vs SERVFAIL ko mix karna galat troubleshooting conclusions deta hai.
real_world_analogy: NOERROR = 'haan yeh ghar milta hai, address yeh hai'; NXDOMAIN = 'yeh address hi exist nahi karta'; SERVFAIL = 'main abhi dhoondh nahi paaya, phone line kat gayi'.
how_it_works: Har response ek 4-bit rcode carry karta hai header byte 3 mein; client us rcode ko dekh kar decide karta hai aage kya karna hai (retry, give up, ya use the answer).
in_this_project: src/wire.ts ka RCODE constant object; src/proxy.ts buildBlockResponse aur handle() ke catch block jo RCODE.SERVFAIL return karta hai.
code_example:
// real, src/wire.ts
export const RCODE = { NOERROR: 0, FORMERR: 1, SERVFAIL: 2, NXDOMAIN: 3, NOTIMP: 4, REFUSED: 5 } as const;
advantages: Standard rcodes se client software predictably behave kar sakta hai
Alag rcodes se debugging aasan hota hai -- kaunsi layer fail hui pata chal jaata hai
disadvantages: Kuch client NXDOMAIN ko aggressively retry karte hain, jo ek design tradeoff bana deta hai (SINK-009 dekhiye)
SERVFAIL bhi client ko retry karne push kar sakta hai, jo upstream failure ke time load badha sakta hai
common_mistakes: NXDOMAIN ko 'error' samajh lena jab woh ek valid, definitive answer hai
SERVFAIL ko hamesha server crash samajh lena
follow_up_questions: FORMERR aur NOTIMP kis situation mein use hote hain is project mein?
Client NXDOMAIN milne par kya karta hai typically?
Negative caching NXDOMAIN ke liye kyun useful hoti hai?

question: What is the basic distinction between a DNS proxy and a DNS resolver, and which one is this project?
answer_hinglish:
Ek RESOLVER apna kaam khud karta hai -- ek naam ko root se shuru karke, authoritative servers se baat karke, step by step resolve karta hai (ya kam se kam ek single trusted upstream ke bina, arbitrary servers se). Ek PROXY resolve nahi karta -- woh beech mein khada hota hai, kuch decisions khud leta hai (block/cache), baaki sab EK configured upstream resolver ko forward kar deta hai jo asal resolution karta hai.

Yeh project ek PROXY hai, resolver nahi -- yeh khud kabhi root/TLD/authoritative servers se baat nahi karta. Yeh sirf ek hi configured upstream (jaise 1.1.1.1) se baat karta hai aur uska jawab relay karta hai, ya khud se ek block jawab bana deta hai.

Is repo ka 15-dns-resolver ek asli RESOLVER hai -- woh arbitrary authoritative servers se baat karta hai aur poora iterative resolution karta hai. Dono projects wire format basics aur TC->TCP pattern share karte hain, par unka JOB alag hai: 15-dns-resolver 'naam resolve karna' hai, yeh project 'relay karna, except blocklist ke against check karna' hai.
why_needed: System design interviews mein yeh distinction baar baar aati hai -- 'kya yeh component resolve kar raha hai ya sirf relay/decide kar raha hai' ek fundamental architecture question hai.
real_world_analogy: Resolver ek detective hai jo khud sabse pooch-taach karke address nikaalta hai; proxy ek receptionist hai jo kuch cases khud handle karti hai (blocklist) aur baaki detective ko forward kar deti hai.
how_it_works: Proxy ke paas sirf ek upstream Endpoint hota hai (SinkholeProxyOptions.upstream); resolver ke paas root hints aur recursive lookup logic hoti hai (jo is project mein kahin nahi hai).
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts SinkholeProxyOptions mein `upstream: Endpoint` sirf EK endpoint hai, multiple authoritative servers ki list nahi.
advantages: Proxy approach simple hai -- resolution complexity kisi aur (upstream) par chhod di
Resolver approach mein kisi third-party upstream par depend nahi karna padta
disadvantages: Proxy upstream ke available hone par depend karta hai -- resolver khud-nirbhar hota hai
Resolver banana kaafi zyada complex hai (referrals, negative caching, DNSSEC, etc.)
common_mistakes: Proxy ko 'chhota resolver' samajhna, jab usme resolution logic hi nahi hai
Yeh maan lena ki proxy bhi root servers se baat kar sakta hai agar zaroorat pade
follow_up_questions: Agar upstream khud down ho, is proxy ka koi fallback hai?
Resolver banane mein sabse zyada complexity kahan aati hai jo proxy mein nahi hai?
Kya ek proxy kabhi resolver ban sakta hai, incrementally?

question: Walk through what happens end to end when a client asks this proxy for an allowed domain for the first time.
answer_hinglish:
Client ek UDP packet bhejta hai proxy ke port (default 15353) par, jisme ek query hoti hai (jaise news.example.com, type A). SinkholeServer ka UDP socket yeh message receive karta hai aur SinkholeProxy.handle(buf) ko pass kar deta hai.

handle() pehle header decode karta hai (12-byte peek), check karta hai ki yeh QR=0 (query hai, response nahi), phir poori query decode karta hai. Domain canonicalize hota hai (lowercase, trailing dot hata kar), aur blocklist.isBlocked() check hota hai -- false aata hai (allowed). Phir cache.get() check hota hai -- pehli baar hai toh MISS.

Ab forwardQuery() call hota hai: upstream ko EXACT client bytes forward hote hain (same transaction id ke saath), UDP par. Upstream se reply aata hai, decodeResponse() se uska header/id/qr verify hota hai, aur agar NOERROR + answers hain toh cache.put() se store hota hai (smallest TTL ke saath). Fir reply RAW BYTES mein client ko wapas bhej diya jaata hai -- stats.forwarded badh jaata hai.
why_needed: Pura request lifecycle ek saath samajhna interview mein 'walk me through a request' type questions ke liye essential hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek courier company ek parcel ko apne hub se bina khole, exact wahi parcel, directly aage bhej de, aur delivery record apne system mein bhi likh le future ke liye.
how_it_works: handle() ek linear decision chain hai: decode -> block check -> cache check -> forward -> cache store -> relay.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts handle() poora yeh flow implement karta hai; src/server.ts bas isko UDP ke upar wrap karta hai.
advantages: Decision chain linear aur predictable hai, samajhna/debug karna aasan
Har step ka apna stat counter hai, observability built-in
disadvantages: Pehli-baar query ka pura cost hota hai (block check + cache miss + full network round trip)
Agar upstream slow hai, client ko bhi wait karna padega (koi stale-while-revalidate nahi)
common_mistakes: Sochna ki cache check block check se PEHLE hoti hai
ID patching ko bhool jaana jab forward ki hui query already client ka ID carry kar rahi hoti hai
follow_up_questions: Pehli baar forward hone par ID ko kyun patch nahi karna padta, par cache hit par karna padta hai?
Agar isi waqt dusra client same domain poochhe, kya race condition ban sakti hai?
Stats counters production mein kaise useful hote?

question: What is the exact blocking rule this project uses -- does blocking a domain also block its parent or sibling domains?
answer_hinglish:
Rule simple hai: ek blocklist entry us EXACT domain aur uski EVERY subdomain ko block karti hai, par kabhi parent ya sibling ko nahi. Jaise `ads.example.com` block karne par `tracker.ads.example.com` bhi block ho jaata hai (woh subdomain hai), par `example.com` (parent) ya `shop.example.com` (sibling) bilkul allowed rehte hain.

Yeh one-directional hai -- subtree neeche ki taraf hi block hoti hai, upar ki taraf nahi. Reason simple: ek tracker company (jaise doubleclick.net) ke paas hazaaron subdomains ho sakte hain, sabko list mein daalna impossible hai, isliye ek parent block karke poori subtree cover kar lete hain. Lekin iska yeh matlab nahi ki agar koi tracker domain kisi legit parent ka subdomain hai, toh parent bhi block ho jaana chahiye.

Is project mein BlockList.isBlocked() yahi rule enforce karta hai -- yeh query ke labels ko TLD-se-shuru karke trie mein walk karta hai, aur jahan bhi ek 'blocked' marked node milta hai (chahe woh exact match ho ya beech mein koi ancestor), wahin se true return ho jaata hai. Order of insertion bhi matter nahi karta -- README ka test 'a shorter listed domain blocks a longer query... independent of insertion order' yehi prove karta hai.
why_needed: Yeh rule hi blocklist ka core contract hai -- galat samjhne se interviewer ko lagega candidate ko basic requirement hi clear nahi hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek building ka pura floor 'restricted' declare kar diya jaaye -- us floor ke sab rooms restricted ho jaate hain, par neeche ya upar ka floor nahi, aur poori building bhi nahi.
how_it_works: Trie mein labels reverse order (TLD first) mein daale jaate hain; lookup bhi wahi order follow karta hai aur pehla 'blocked' node milte hi ruk jaata hai.
in_this_project: src/blocklist.ts BlockList.isBlocked(): labels ko reverse order mein walk karta hai, `if (node.blocked) return true;` jahan milta hai turant return.
advantages: Ek entry se poori subdomain tree cover ho jaati hai -- maintenance kam
Rule predictable aur explainable hai -- kabhi 'surprise' overblocking nahi
disadvantages: Agar ek legit service kisi blocked domain ke subdomain par host ho jaaye, woh bhi block ho jayega
Allowlist/exception ka koi concept nahi hai abhi -- ek baar block, hamesha block
common_mistakes: Sochna ki parent bhi block ho jaata hai jab child block karo
Insertion order par depend karna, jab actually woh matter nahi karta
follow_up_questions: Agar `example.com` aur `ads.example.com` dono list mein ho, kya duplicate node banta hai?
Allowlist exception add karna ho (block parent but allow one specific subdomain), is design mein kaisa change hoga?
Case-sensitivity ka kya role hai is rule mein?

question: What are the two block-response modes (NXDOMAIN vs sinkhole IP), and what is the real tradeoff between them?
answer_hinglish:
Blocked domain ka jawab dene ke do configurable tareeke hain. 'nxdomain' mode mein proxy bolta hai NXDOMAIN -- 'yeh naam exist hi nahi karta', technically sabse correct answer. 'sinkhole' mode mein proxy ek NOERROR jawab deta hai ek configured A record ke saath (default 0.0.0.0) -- ek 'jhooth', jaise naam resolve ho gaya ho par ek useless address par.

Tradeoff real hai, dressed-up choice nahi: kuch client software NXDOMAIN ko 'try again' jaisa treat karta hai aur AGGRESSIVELY retry karta hai -- ek single blocked ad request burst-of-retries mein badal sakta hai, jo useless network traffic hai. Sinkhole IP ek lie hai, par zyadatar clients ek normal-dikhne-wale answer ko FINAL maan lete hain aur retry nahi karte -- kam traffic, par technically galat jawab.

Pi-hole khud yeh exact dilemma face karta hai aur isi liye dono options deta hai configurable settings ki tarah -- is project mein bhi yehi approach hai (`SinkholeProxyOptions.mode`). Ek important detail: sinkholing SIRF A query types ke liye implement hai; AAAA ya koi aur type sinkhole mode mein bhi NXDOMAIN hi paata hai (PLAN.md 'Not in scope').
why_needed: Yeh ek classic 'no free lunch' design decision hai jo interviewer ko dikhata hai ki candidate real tradeoffs samajhta hai, sirf feature list nahi raTTa hai.
real_world_analogy: NXDOMAIN jaise ek phone number 'disconnected' bolna (kuch log turant dobara dial karte hain), sinkhole jaise phone ring hone dena par koi uthaye nahi (zyadatar log samajh jaate hain koi nahi hai).
how_it_works: buildBlockResponse() mode aur query type dono check karta hai: nxdomain mode ya non-A type -> NXDOMAIN; sinkhole mode + A type -> ek encodeARecord() se bana A record, NOERROR ke saath.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts buildBlockResponse(): `if (this.mode === "nxdomain" || q.type !== TYPE.A) { return encodeMessage(base(RCODE.NXDOMAIN, [q]), [q], []); }` baaki sinkhole A record banata hai.
advantages: NXDOMAIN technically correct hai, standard-compliant
Sinkhole IP mode kam client-side retries generate karta hai
disadvantages: NXDOMAIN kuch clients mein retry storms cause kar sakta hai
Sinkhole IP ek lie hai -- ek observant client/tool 'suspicious' flag laga sakta hai
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki sinkhole mode HAR query type ke liye A record deta hai
NXDOMAIN aur SERVFAIL ko same severity ka maan lena client-retry-behavior ke liye
follow_up_questions: AAAA sinkholing add karni ho (:: address), kahan change isolate hoga?
Kaunsa mode production mein zyada common hai aur kyun?

question: Why does the cache count the TTL down on every read instead of just returning the original stored TTL value?
answer_hinglish:
Real DNS resolvers ka cache behavior yeh hota hai: agar ek answer 300-second TTL ke saath store hua, aur koi client 50 second baad usi naam ko poochhe, toh use 250 (300-50) milna chahiye, 300 nahi. Yeh batata hai 'is jawab ka itna time aur bacha hai', jo client ko sahi decide karne deta hai ki kab dobara poochhna hai.

Agar hum original stale TTL hamesha return karte, toh client sochega jawab abhi fresh store hua hai, jab ki asal mein woh kaafi der se cache mein hai -- client apna khud ka caching/retry timing galat calculate karega, aur agar woh value aage forward karta hai (jaise ek dusra resolver chain mein), total system ka freshness guarantee toot jaata.

Is project mein ResponseCache har entry ke saath uske answer records ke TTL fields ke exact BYTE OFFSETS bhi store karta hai (ttlOffsets). get() call par, elapsedSeconds nikalta hai (`Math.floor((now - insertedAt)/1000)`), aur har offset par 4-byte TTL field ko `Math.max(0, original - elapsedSeconds)` se overwrite karta hai COPY buffer mein -- original stored buffer kabhi mutate nahi hota. Yeh real resolver jaisa hi behavior deta hai, bina ek parsed-record representation maintain kiye.
why_needed: Yeh ek subtle lekin high-value correctness detail hai -- interview mein yeh pucha jaana common hai kyunki naive cache implementations isse miss karte hain.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek parking ticket par 'abhi se 2 ghante valid' likha ho, par jab tum ticket dekho 1 ghanta baad, usme likha hona chahiye '1 ghanta bacha hai', na ki fir se '2 ghante'.
how_it_works: Har answer ka ttlOffset wire.ts decodeResponse() mein record kiya jaata hai; cache.get() us exact offset par 4-byte integer ko decrement karta hai har read par.
in_this_project: src/cache.ts get(): `const elapsedSeconds = Math.floor((this.clock.now() - e.insertedAt) / 1000); for (const offset of e.ttlOffsets) { ... out.writeUInt32BE(Math.max(0, original - elapsedSeconds), offset); }`
advantages: Client ko bilkul real-resolver-jaisa accurate TTL milta hai
Koi parsed-record representation maintain nahi karna padta, raw bytes par hi patch ho jaata hai
disadvantages: Har get() par ek buffer copy aur chhoti CPU cost lagti hai
Floor(elapsed/1000) se sub-second precision loss hota hai, par DNS TTL seconds mein hi hota hai
common_mistakes: Original buffer ko directly mutate karna (cache ke andar wala), jo dusre readers ko corrupt kar dega
TTL ko negative hone dena jab elapsed > original TTL (floor zero zaroori hai)
follow_up_questions: Do clients SAME query thoda alag time par karein, dono ko kya TTL dikhna chahiye?
Yeh countdown rdata ke kisi field par kyun safe NAHI hota, sirf TTL par safe hai?
Agar elapsedSeconds TTL se bada ho jaaye floor se pehle, kya ho sakta tha?

question: How does a forwarded (non-blocked, non-cached) query get relayed back to the client with the client's own transaction id?
answer_hinglish:
Jab query blocklist mein nahi hoti aur cache mein bhi nahi milti, proxy use upstream ko forward karta hai -- aur yahan EK important choice hai: client ka ORIGINAL query buffer (jisme uska apna transaction ID already hota hai) WAISE KA WAISA upstream ko bhej diya jaata hai, bina ID badle. Isliye jab upstream reply karta hai, uska reply bhi WAHI ID carry karta hai -- koi patching ki zaroorat hi nahi padti pehli-baar-forward ke case mein, upstream ka raw reply seedha client ko relay ho jaata hai.

Yeh design isliye chalta hai kyunki har forwarded query apna EK naya, ephemeral UDP socket leta hai jo sirf USI query ke liye hai -- isliye multiplexing ki koi zaroorat nahi, aur ID rewrite karne ka koi fayda nahi (15-dns-resolver jaise long-lived shared socket mein ID rewrite zaroori hota hai, kyunki wahan EK socket se MANY concurrent lookups chal rahe hote hain).

Cache HIT ka case alag hai: wahan stored response ek PURANI query ke liye the (jis ID se original store hua), par abhi ek NAYA client apna khud ka ID leke aaya hai -- isliye patchId() se sirf 2-byte ID field patch hota hai cached copy mein, baaki sab bytes untouched.
why_needed: Yeh samajhna zaroori hai ki ID handling forward-path aur cache-hit-path mein ALAG hai -- interview mein yeh confusion common hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek courier parcel jisme pehle se hi ek tracking number (ID) likha hai -- agar seedha bhej rahe ho to number wahi rehta hai; par agar ek PURANA saved parcel label reuse kar rahe ho naye order ke liye, to label ka number badalna padega.
how_it_works: Forward path: raw buf as-is bhejte hain, ID already correct hai. Cache-hit path: patchId(cachedBuf, rawHeader.id) se sirf pehle 2 bytes overwrite hote hain.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts handle(): forward ke liye `forwardQuery(buf, ...)` seedha raw buf bhejta hai; cache hit ke liye `return patchId(cached, rawHeader.id);`
advantages: Forward path mein ID rewrite ka koi overhead nahi -- kam code, kam bugs
Cache-hit path mein sirf 2 bytes patch karna hai, pura buffer re-encode nahi karna
disadvantages: Design assume karta hai har forward apna socket leta hai -- agar kabhi socket pooling add ho, yeh assumption todni padegi
Ek chhoti patch logic bhi galat offset par likh di jaaye toh poora packet corrupt ho sakta hai
common_mistakes: Forward path mein bhi ID patch karne ki koshish karna, jab zaroorat hi nahi hai
Cache hit par poora packet re-encode karna jab sirf 2-byte patch kaafi hai
follow_up_questions: Agar kabhi socket pooling/multiplexing add ho, ID handling kaise badlega?
patchId() kyun sirf 2 bytes touch karta hai, poora header kyun nahi?
Kya transaction ID ka mismatch koi security implication rakhta hai yahan?

question: What does SERVFAIL mean in this project, and under exactly which conditions is it returned?
answer_hinglish:
SERVFAIL ek signal hai 'main is query ko successfully process nahi kar paaya' -- naam valid hai ya nahi, pata nahi chala, kyunki hum upstream tak successfully pahunch hi nahi paaye ya upstream ka jawab bharosemand nahi tha. Yeh kabhi 'crash' ya 'hang' nahi hona chahiye -- client ko turant ek definitive signal milna chahiye taaki woh retry ya give-up decide kar sake.

Is project mein SERVFAIL teen specific conditions mein aata hai, sab proxy.ts ke handle() ke try/catch ke andar: (1) upstream timeout ho jaaye (TimeoutError), (2) upstream se koi network/transport error aaye (TransportError, jaise connection refused), ya (3) upstream ka reply decode ho jaaye par uska QR bit ya transaction ID client ki original query se match na kare -- yeh teesra case khaas tarah se important hai, kyunki yahan humein EK answer mil chuka hota hai, par woh BHAROSEMAND nahi hai, isliye use RELAY nahi karte, use discard karke SERVFAIL bhejte hain.

Teeno case mein stats.servfail++ hota hai aur response KABHI cache nahi hota (sirf NOERROR + answers > 0 wale successful forwards cache hote hain).
why_needed: SERVFAIL ki exact trigger conditions samajhna debugging ke liye critical hai -- 'client ko SERVFAIL mil raha hai' ek common production symptom hai jiska root cause alag-alag ho sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek operator kehta hai 'maine try kiya lekin line hi nahi lagi, ya jo bhi jawab mila woh kisi aur ke sawaal ka tha' -- woh definitely NAHI bolega 'yeh number exist nahi karta' (woh NXDOMAIN hota), balki 'mujhe pata nahi, try nahi ho paaya'.
how_it_works: handle() ka try block forwardQuery() aur decodeResponse() dono ko wrap karta hai; koi bhi throw (TimeoutError, TransportError, ya id/qr mismatch wala WireError) catch mein jaake SERVFAIL ban jaata hai.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts handle() catch block: `catch { this.stats.servfail++; return encodeMessage(base(RCODE.SERVFAIL, [q]), [q], []); }`; id/qr check: `if (!parsed.header.qr || parsed.header.id !== rawHeader.id) throw new WireError(...)`
advantages: Ek single catch block se saari failure modes handle hoti hain consistently
Kabhi galat/mismatched answer client ko relay nahi hota
disadvantages: Client ko exact reason nahi pata chalta (timeout vs mismatch vs transport error sab SERVFAIL hi dikhte hain)
Repeated SERVFAIL retries upstream par extra load bana sakte hain agar upstream khud slow hai
common_mistakes: Mismatched id/QR wale reply ko bhi 'successful forward' samajh kar relay kar dena
SERVFAIL response ko accidentally cache kar dena
follow_up_questions: SERVFAIL ko log karke alert kaise design karoge production mein?
Kya SERVFAIL responses ko bhi short TTL ke saath cache karna chahiye (negative caching jaisa)?
Agar upstream consistently SERVFAIL de raha ho, proxy kya alag kar sakta hai (circuit breaker jaisa)?

question: Why is sinkholing implemented only for A-type queries, with every other query type getting NXDOMAIN in both modes?
answer_hinglish:
Sinkhole mode ka pura idea hai ek 'normal-dikhne-wala' jawab dena taaki client retry na kare. Par 'normal-dikhne-wala' jawab banane ke liye proxy ko us record type ka ENCODER chahiye -- is project mein sirf A record ka encoder (encodeARecord) built hai, kyunki yeh scope-cut deliberate hai (PLAN.md 'Not in scope': AAAA aur har doosra type ka sinkholing abhi nahi hai).

Isliye jab query type A nahi hai (jaise AAAA, MX, TXT), proxy ke paas koi tareeka hi nahi hai ek 'fake par valid' jawab banane ka us type ke liye -- toh woh fallback karta hai NXDOMAIN par, CHAHE mode 'sinkhole' hi set ho. Yeh ek honest limitation hai, feature nahi -- Pi-hole ka bhi historical default AAAA ke liye NXDOMAIN hi tha, isliye yeh ek defensible, simple choice hai, 100% feature-complete nahi.

buildBlockResponse() mein yeh ek single condition se enforce hota hai: `if (this.mode === "nxdomain" || q.type !== TYPE.A)`. Yeh line dono conditions ko OR se jodti hai -- mode nxdomain ho YA type A na ho, dono cases NXDOMAIN milta hai.
why_needed: Yeh ek 'what's NOT implemented and why' question hai, jo honesty aur scope-awareness dikhata hai -- exactly jo brief maang rahi hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek dukaan sirf ek product ke liye 'fake display model' rakhti hai (A record), baaki products ke liye seedha bol deti hai 'stock mein nahi hai' (NXDOMAIN), kyunki fake model banana sirf us ek product ke liye possible tha.
how_it_works: buildBlockResponse() ek single `if` check se A-vs-non-A aur mode dono handle karta hai, encodeARecord() sirf tab call hota hai jab dono conditions false hon.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts buildBlockResponse(); src/wire.ts encodeARecord (yehi ek encoder exist karta hai sinkhole answers ke liye); PLAN.md 'Not in scope' section.
advantages: Scope chhota rakha gaya -- koi AAAA/MX/TXT encoder maintain nahi karna padta
Behavior predictable hai -- jo bhi feature missing hai woh explicitly documented hai
disadvantages: AAAA queries wale clients (IPv6-first) ko blocked domain ke liye NXDOMAIN milta hai, sinkhole IP nahi -- inconsistent experience IPv4 vs IPv6 clients ke beech
AAAA sinkholing add karni ho toh ek naya encoder (:: address ke liye) likhna padega
common_mistakes: Sochna ki 'sinkhole' mode set karne se SAB query types ke liye ek fake jawab milta hai
AAAA ko A jaisa hi treat kar dena is codebase mein, jab A-only encoder hai
follow_up_questions: AAAA sinkholing add karna kitna bada change hoga, kahan isolate hoga?
Kya yeh inconsistency (IPv4 sinkhole, IPv6 NXDOMAIN) production mein problem bana sakti hai?
MX ya TXT queries ke liye sinkholing kaisi dikhegi, kya woh meaningful bhi hai?

question: How does this proxy handle malformed or unusual queries -- what decides between silently dropping, FORMERR, and NOTIMP?
answer_hinglish:
Proxy har galat/unusual query ko 'closest real-DNS answer' deta hai, crash kabhi nahi. Rules order mein hain: (1) 12 bytes se kam -- header hi complete nahi hai, silently DROP (kuch bhi reply nahi bhejte, kyunki hum ID tak nahi padh sakte confidently). (2) QR=1 (yeh ek response hai, query nahi) -- silently DROP, taaki do misconfigured servers ek dusre ka output kabhi 'ping-pong' na karein. (3) Query decode ho jaaye par opcode QUERY nahi hai -- NOTIMP ('yeh operation support nahi hai'). (4) Zero ya do-se-zyada questions -- FORMERR ('packet format hi galat hai'). (5) Question class IN nahi hai -- NOTIMP.

Yeh hierarchy isliye hai kyunki har case ka 'severity' alag hai: header-level truncation itna basic hai ki ID bhi trust nahi kar sakte (drop safest hai); ek valid-looking query jo humein samajh nahi aati (wrong opcode/class) NOTIMP deserve karti hai; aur ek structurally invalid packet (galat question count) FORMERR deserve karta hai.

handle() mein yeh checks EK-ke-baad-EK hote hain: pehle decodeHeader() (QR check), phir decodeQuery() (WireError par FORMERR), phir opcode check (NOTIMP), phir question count/class check. Proxy.test.ts ka 'malformed and unusual queries' suite (5 tests) aur invariant.test.ts ke 1500 random + 500 bit-flipped packets (wire.test.ts se) yeh prove karte hain ki koi bhi combination crash nahi karti.
why_needed: Untrusted network input ko correctly aur safely handle karna ek senior-level concern hai -- yeh dikhata hai candidate 'happy path' se aage soch sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek receptionist: agar koi aadha-adhoora form de (bina naam likhe), woh seedha ignore kar degi; agar form valid hai par kisi ANOKHI language mein hai jo woh samajhti nahi, 'main yeh handle nahi kar sakti' bolegi; agar form mein do baar 'naam' field bhara hai jo ek hi field honi chahiye, 'yeh form hi galat bhara hai' bolegi.
how_it_works: Har check apna specific rcode return karta hai; drop ke case mein function `undefined` return karta hai jisse server.ts kuch bhi nahi bhejta.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts handle(): `if (rawHeader.qr) return undefined;`, catch block se FORMERR, `if (query.header.opcode !== OPCODE_QUERY) return ... NOTIMP`, `if (!q || query.questions.length !== 1) return ... FORMERR`, `if (q.class !== CLASS_IN) return ... NOTIMP`.
advantages: Har edge case ka ek defined, standard-compliant behavior hai
Ping-pong loop (QR=1 drop) jaisi production outage prevent karta hai
disadvantages: Itne saare sequential checks maintain karna slightly verbose hai
Silently drop karna (bina kuch reply ke) debugging ke liye thoda opaque ho sakta hai agar logging nahi hai
common_mistakes: QR=1 drop check hata dena -- do misconfigured DNS servers ek doosre ka output infinite loop mein bhejte reh sakte
FORMERR aur NOTIMP ko interchangeable samajhna
follow_up_questions: QR=1 drop check hatane se exact kya scenario ban sakta hai do misconfigured servers ke beech?
12-byte se kam packet ko FORMERR kyun nahi, drop kyun?
Is layered validation ko kaise test karoge taaki har branch genuinely exercise ho (not just 'caught by an earlier check')?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Layered validation (sequential ifs) simple hai par order-dependent -- agar koi check reorder ho jaaye, behavior badal sakta hai silently. Ek alternative ek single validation function with explicit priority table ho sakta hai, jo order ko explicit documentation banata hai, par extra abstraction cost deta hai is chhoti scale par.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar QR=1 drop check hata diya jaaye, aur yeh proxy kisi aur misconfigured server ke saath network mein ho jo bhi responses ko queries samajh leta hai, dono systems ek dusre ka output infinite loop mein forward karte reh sakte hain -- bandwidth aur CPU dono waste.
advanced.alternatives: Kuch resolvers rate-limit karte hain malformed packets ko (per-source), taaki ek buggy client flood na kar sake; yahan abhi koi rate limiting nahi hai, sirf loopback-bind guard hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: High query volume par, har malformed packet ek chhoti CPU cost hai (decode attempt + encode response) -- 10x/100x par yeh cost linearly badhti hai; agar attacker intentionally malformed packets flood kare, yeh ek amplification/DoS vector ban sakta hai bina rate limiting ke.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein ek per-source rate limiter add karna, malformed-query count ko metrics mein expose karna (abuse detection ke liye), aur shayad structured logging add karna taaki silent drops bhi observable rahen.

question: How exactly does the trie over reversed dot-labels work, and how does a lookup walk it?
answer_hinglish:
Trie ek tree structure hai jahan har node ka ek Map<string, TrieNode> hota hai (label -> child node) aur ek `blocked` boolean flag. Domain insert karte waqt, naam ko labels mein split karte hain (`ads.example.com` -> ['ads','example','com']), aur ise TLD-FIRST order mein insert karte hain -- matlab path hota hai root -> 'com' -> 'example' -> 'ads', aur 'ads' node par `blocked = true` set hota hai.

Lookup bhi EXACT same order follow karta hai: query ke labels bhi TLD-first walk kiye jaate hain (array ko reverse-index se iterate karke, bina naya array banaye) -- `for (let i = labels.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)`. Har step par current node se agla child dhoondha jaata hai (`node.children.get(labels[i])`); agar child na mile, lookup turant false return kar deta hai (naam blocklist mein bilkul nahi hai, na khud na koi ancestor). Agar child mile aur woh node 'blocked' marked hai, turant TRUE return hota hai -- isse age ke labels check karne ki zaroorat hi nahi (jo bhi ab aata hai woh us blocked node ka subdomain hai).

Shared suffix ka fayda yahan dikhta hai: `a.doubleclick.net` aur `b.doubleclick.net` dono SAME 'net' -> 'doubleclick' path share karte hain trie mein -- sirf ek baar banaya jaata hai, dono ke liye.
why_needed: Yeh is project ka core data structure hai -- interview mein trie internals clearly explain karna (insert order, walk direction, early-exit) candidate ki data-structure clarity dikhata hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek file system path -- `/com/example/ads` folder ko 'restricted' mark karo, aur koi bhi file jo `/com/example/ads/...` ke andar hai automatically restricted hai, bina har file ko individually mark kiye.
how_it_works: Insert: TLD-first path banate hue missing nodes create karte hain, aakhri node par blocked=true. Lookup: wahi path walk karo, pehla 'blocked' node milte hi true return karo.
in_this_project: src/blocklist.ts BlockList.add() aur isBlocked(), dono `labels.length - 1` se `0` tak loop karte hain (TLD first); TrieNode interface `{ children: Map<string, TrieNode>; blocked: boolean }`.
advantages: Lookup ek baar labels walk karta hai, O(number of labels), no re-hashing of full strings
Shared suffixes memory mein ek hi baar store hote hain
disadvantages: Har node ek Map object hai -- bahut chhote blocklists (kuch hi entries) ke liye Set se zyada memory overhead ho sakta hai
Trie ko traverse karne ke liye pointer-chasing hoti hai, jo CPU cache ke liye Set ke contiguous hash table se thoda worse ho sakta hai chhoti scale par
common_mistakes: Labels ko normal order (left-to-right) mein insert karna, jo subdomain-matching rule todta hai
Lookup ko poora path walk karne ke baad check karna, jab early-exit (`if (node.blocked) return true`) zaroori hai
follow_up_questions: Million-domain blocklist ke liye trie ka memory footprint Set se kitna alag hoga?
Agar ek node ke multiple children ho (jaise 100 subdomains ek level par), Map lookup ka cost kya hai?
Wildcard domains (jaise `*.ads.com` explicitly) ko kaise represent karte, agar sirf subdomain-wildcard na chahiye ho?

question: How does decodeResponse read just enough of an upstream answer (name/type/class/ttl) while skipping rdata by length?
answer_hinglish:
decodeResponse() header aur questions normal tareeke se decode karta hai, phir ancount jitne answer records ke liye ek loop chalaata hai. Har answer record ke liye, pehle naam decode hota hai (r.name(), jo compression pointers bhi handle karta hai), phir type (u16), class (u16). Yahaan ek IMPORTANT detail hai: TTL field padhne se PEHLE current position (`r.pos`) ko `ttlOffset` mein save kar liya jaata hai -- yeh exact BYTE offset hai jahan 4-byte TTL integer shuru hota hai.

TTL (u32) padha jaata hai, phir rdlength (u16) padha jaata hai -- yeh batata hai rdata kitne bytes ka hai. Is point ke baad, rdata ko INTERPRET nahi kiya jaata -- sirf `r.skip(rdlength, "rdata")` call hoti hai, jo Reader ki position ko aage badha deti hai bina rdata ke content ko dekhe bhi. Yeh deliberate hai: rdata ke andar ek compressed name pointer ho sakta hai jo sirf ORIGINAL packet ke exact bytes ke relative valid hai -- usse interpret karna, ya naye packet mein copy karna, pointer ko wrong offset bana sakta.

Aakhir mein `{ name, type, class: klass, ttl, ttlOffset }` ek AnswerMeta object banta hai -- yeh wahi 'enough' information hai jo cache ko TTL countdown ke liye chahiye (SINK-010 dekhiye), bina rdata samjhe.
why_needed: Yeh is project ka single sabse important design implementation detail hai -- 'minimal decode, skip the rest by length' ka exact mechanism samajhna, jo poore relay-raw-bytes decision ko possible banata hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek customs officer ek parcel ka label (naam, type, weight) padh leta hai scanning ke liye, par parcel ke ANDAR ka saara content nahi kholta -- sirf 'itna weight hai, itna space lega' maan leta hai aur aage bhej deta hai.
how_it_works: Reader class ka pos field sequentially aage badhta hai; ttlOffset ek snapshot hai us position ka TTL field se exactly PEHLE.
in_this_project: src/wire.ts decodeResponse(): `const ttlOffset = r.pos; const ttl = r.u32("RR ttl"); const rdlength = r.u16("RR rdlength"); r.skip(rdlength, "rdata");`
advantages: Koi RR-type-specific decoder likhne ki zaroorat nahi -- CNAME/NS/MX/SOA/PTR sab kuch skip ho jaata hai uniformly
ttlOffset record karne se cache ko exact patch-point mil jaata hai without re-scanning
disadvantages: Agar kabhi rdata ke andar ki info chahiye ho (jaise CNAME follow karna), yeh approach kaam nahi karega bina naya decoder likhe
Ek galat rdlength (corrupt/malicious upstream se) poori baaki records ki parsing ko misalign kar sakta hai
common_mistakes: ttlOffset ko TTL padhne ke BAAD record karna, jo galat offset de dega
Rdata ko 'thodi der ke liye' interpret karne ki koshish karna 'sirf dekh lete hain' soch kar
follow_up_questions: Agar full RR decoding add karni ho (jaise CNAME follow karne wali allowlist feature), kya naye risks introduce honge?
Rdlength galat ho (bahut bada) toh Reader kya karega?
Authority/additional sections ko bilkul skip karne ka kya tradeoff hai?

question: Explain the ResponseCache's stored-byte-offset trick for TTL countdown in detail -- why is this safe here specifically?
answer_hinglish:
Jab ek upstream reply cache mein store hota hai, ResponseCache.put() sirf raw bytes copy nahi karta -- woh `ttlOffsets: number[]` bhi store karta hai, jo har answer record ke TTL field ka EXACT byte position hai (wire.ts se decodeResponse() ne yeh already nikaal rakha hai). Yeh ek 'pointer into a buffer' trick hai -- hum poora record parse/re-encode nahi karte, sirf yaad rakhte hain 'TTL yahan hai'.

Safe kyun hai: TTL ek FIXED-WIDTH 4-byte unsigned integer hai, aur uske AASPAAS koi name compression ya variable-length encoding nahi hoti -- woh bas 4 raw bytes hain jo ek number represent karte hain. Isliye use-in-place overwrite karna (naya number likh dena) kisi doosre field ko kabhi corrupt nahi karta. Yeh EXACTLY opposite hai rdata ke case se (jahan hum kabhi kuch touch nahi karte), kyunki rdata ke andar variable-length aur compression pointer ho sakte hain jinka meaning unke EXACT original position se juda hota hai.

get() call par: `out.readUInt32BE(offset)` se original TTL padha jaata hai, elapsed time se decrement hota hai (`Math.max(0, original - elapsedSeconds)`), aur `out.writeUInt32BE(...)` se WAPAS usi offset par likh diya jaata hai -- ek COPY buffer mein, original cached buffer kabhi touch nahi hota.
why_needed: Yeh dikhata hai ki candidate samajhta hai 'kyun yeh specific optimization safe hai' -- generic 'cache mein byte offset store karo' nahi, balki 'kyun TTL field ke liye yeh safe hai aur rdata ke liye nahi' wali nuanced understanding.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek parking garage ka digital display board jisme sirf 'baki minutes' ka number hota hai, ek fixed-size LED segment par -- woh number update karna aasan hai bina poore board ka design badle, kyunki woh field hamesha fixed jagah par hai aur fixed format mein hai.
how_it_works: Put time par offset record hota hai (decodeResponse se), get time par wahi offset use karke read-modify-write hota hai buffer ke copy par.
in_this_project: src/cache.ts Entry interface mein `ttlOffsets: number[]`; put() aur get() dono isi field ko use karte hain.
advantages: Koi re-parse/re-encode nahi lagta read par, sirf chhoti fixed-size field patch hoti hai
Multiple answer records ka TTL EK saath countdown ho jaata hai, ek array of offsets se
disadvantages: Yeh trick sirf fixed-width, compression-free fields ke liye hi generalize hoti hai -- har field ke liye yeh approach kaam nahi karegi
Agar offsets galat record hon (bug), TTL ki jagah kisi aur field ko corrupt kar sakte hain silently
common_mistakes: Sochna ki yeh trick kisi bhi field ke liye use ki ja sakti hai -- yeh sirf un fields ke liye safe hai jo fixed-width hain aur name-compression se door hain
Original cached buffer ko directly modify karna get() mein, jo next read ko bhi affect karega
follow_up_questions: Yeh same technique kis aur fixed-width field par use ki ja sakti hai is wire format mein?
Agar ek hi reply mein alag-alag TTL wale multiple answers ho, countdown sab par EK saath kaise apply hota hai?
Buffer.from(e.buf) copy lena kyun zaroori hai get() mein?

question: What is lazy expiry in this cache, and how does it compare to running a periodic eviction sweep?
answer_hinglish:
Lazy expiry ka matlab hai: expired entries ko koi background process proactively remove NAHI karta. Ek entry sirf tab 'notice' hoti hai jab koi usi exact (name, type) key ke liye dobara query kare -- get() check karta hai `e.expiresAt <= now`, aur agar expired hai, usi waqt delete kar deta hai (`this.entries.delete(k)`), warna miss jaisa treat karta hai.

Iske against option hota hai ek PERIODIC SWEEP -- ek timer (setInterval jaisa) jo har kuch second mein saari entries check karke expired wali hata de, chahe koi unhe query kare ya nahi. Sweep ka fayda yeh hai ki memory jaldi free hoti hai; nuksan yeh hai ki usko apna khud ka LIFECYCLE chahiye hota -- kaun start kare, kaun stop kare (jab proxy band ho), kis Clock se time le jab koi active request nahi hai -- yeh sab extra design aur testing surface hai.

Is project mein lazy expiry choose kiya gaya hai (23-password-manager ke session idle timeout jaisi hi reasoning): koi downside nahi hai important practical sense mein, kyunki ek expired-but-never-asked-again entry memory mein thodi der zyada reh jaana koi problem nahi hai -- aur `maxEntries` (oldest-insertion-evicted-first) ek upper bound laga deta hai total memory par, isliye yeh ek 'infinite leak' nahi ban sakta.
why_needed: Lazy-vs-sweep ek classic caching tradeoff hai jo almost har system design interview mein aata hai -- yahan iska concrete, project-specific justification dena zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek library jo kitaabon ko sirf tab check karti hai ki woh 'overdue' hain jab koi unhe dhoondhne aata hai, bajaye har ghante har kitaab check karne ke -- kaam kam hota hai, par ek overdue kitaab shelf par thodi der zyada reh sakti hai.
how_it_works: get() hi expiry ka SOLE checkpoint hai; put() sirf naya expiresAt set karta hai aur maxEntries exceed hone par oldest entry evict karta hai.
in_this_project: src/cache.ts get(): `if (e.expiresAt <= this.clock.now()) { this.entries.delete(k); return undefined; }`; evict() private method jo sirf size-bound maintain karta hai, TTL expiry se related nahi hai.
advantages: Koi timer lifecycle manage nahi karna padta -- simpler code, kam testing surface
maxEntries se memory bounded rehti hai even without active sweep
disadvantages: Ek expired entry jo kabhi dobara query nahi hoti, maxEntries tak reach hone tak memory mein reh sakti hai
Memory usage thoda unpredictable ho sakta hai agar bahut saari entries expire ho jaayein par kabhi evict na hon
common_mistakes: Lazy expiry ko 'memory leak' samajh lena, jab maxEntries use bound kar deta hai
Sweep ko hamesha 'better' maan lena, jab usme real lifecycle cost hoti hai
follow_up_questions: maxEntries na hota toh lazy expiry kitna risky ho jaata?
Kis scale par periodic sweep add karna justified ho jaata?
Oldest-insertion eviction (LRU nahi) ka yahan kya tradeoff hai?

question: Why does every forwarded query get its own ephemeral UDP socket instead of sharing one long-lived socket?
answer_hinglish:
Har forwarded query ke liye `queryUdp()` ek BILKUL NAYA UDP socket banata hai (`dgram.createSocket("udp4")`), use bind karta hai (port 0 = OS choose kare), query bhejta hai, reply ka wait karta hai, aur phir socket ko CLOSE kar deta hai -- chahe success ho ya fail/timeout.

Yeh design isliye chuna gaya hai kyunki is proxy mein EK socket sirf EK query ko serve karta hai -- koi multiplexing nahi chahiye. Agar iske bajaye EK long-lived shared socket hoti (jaise 15-dns-resolver ka resolver socket, jo MANY concurrent lookups ko ek shared infrastructure se serve karta hai), toh us socket ko pata hona chahiye 'kaunsa incoming reply kis pending query ka hai' -- jiske liye transaction IDs ko track/rewrite karna padta, kyunki concurrent queries clash kar sakte the same ID par.

Ephemeral-per-query design mein yeh problem hi nahi aati: socket khud ek dedicated 'conversation channel' hai, aur `rinfo.address !== to.host || rinfo.port !== to.port` check (wrong-source-address defense) bhi isi socket ke context mein simple reh jaata hai -- sirf yeh dekhna hai ki reply SAHI upstream se aaya. Cost yeh hai ki har query ek socket create/bind/close ka chhota overhead leta hai, par given ki queries already network-bound hain, yeh overhead negligible hai.
why_needed: Socket-per-request vs shared-socket-with-multiplexing ek common infra design choice hai -- interview mein 'kyun yeh simpler design yahan chalta hai' samajhna zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek disposable phone line sirf ek call ke liye lena, use karke phenk dena -- kabhi confuse nahi hoga ki yeh call kis conversation ka hissa hai, bajaye ek shared office line par multiple calls track karne ke.
how_it_works: queryUdp() socket lifecycle (`sock.bind` -> `sock.send` -> `sock.on('message')` -> `sock.close()`) poori tarah ek single Promise ke andar scoped hai.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts queryUdp(): har call apna `dgram.createSocket("udp4")` banata hai aur `finish()` helper mein `sock.close()` call hota hai.
advantages: Koi ID-rewriting/multiplexing logic nahi chahiye -- simpler, kam bugs
Ek query ka failure doosri queries ko kabhi affect nahi karta (isolated sockets)
disadvantages: High query-rate par socket create/bind/close ka overhead accumulate ho sakta hai
OS-level ephemeral port exhaustion theoretically possible hai bahut high concurrency par
common_mistakes: Sochna ki yeh design high-throughput production DNS server ke liye bhi best hai, jab EK socket pooling se better throughput mil sakta
Socket close() bhool jaana error path mein (yahan `finish()` helper isse guarantee karta hai)
follow_up_questions: Bahut high query rate par (jaise 10000 qps), yeh design kaise bottleneck ban sakta hai?
Agar socket pooling add karni ho, ID multiplexing kaise design karoge?
Socket na close hone ka kya risk hai is design mein?

question: How does readName's compression-pointer handling guarantee decoding always terminates, even on a hostile packet?
answer_hinglish:
readName() ek naam decode karta hai jo labels aur/ya compression pointers ka mix ho sakta hai. Do independent loop-protection rules hain (15-dns-resolver se reused idea): (1) ek pointer STRICTLY BACKWARDS point karna chahiye -- `if (target >= runStart) throw` -- matlab jahan abhi hum labels padh rahe hain usse PEHLE hi point karna chahiye, kabhi aage ya khud par nahi. (2) Per-naam MAX_POINTER_JUMPS (32) se zyada pointers follow nahi kar sakte.

Yeh dono mil kar GUARANTEE dete hain ki decoding kabhi infinite loop mein nahi phasegi: Rule 1 ensure karta hai ki har jump ka target STRICTLY chhota hota hai pichle 'run start' se -- isliye targets ek strictly-decreasing sequence banate hain, jo buffer ki finite length ke andar sirf FINITE baar ho sakta hai (0 se shuru hoke neeche hi jaa sakta hai, upar nahi). Rule 2 ek EXTRA hard cap hai, chahe Rule 1 ke bawajood bhi kisi tarah bahut saari chhoti jumps ho jaayein, 32 se zyada allowed nahi.

`runStart` variable yeh track karta hai ki 'is CURRENT run ki shuruaat kahan thi', aur har jump ke baad yeh update hota hai target ke barabar -- isliye agla pointer PEHLE se bhi pehle point karna hoga. Yeh elegant hai kyunki ek single comparison (`target >= runStart`) hi backward-only guarantee enforce karta hai, bina kisi 'visited set' ya extra memory ke.
why_needed: Yeh ek classic adversarial-input-safety question hai -- compression pointers DNS parsing ka sabse exploit-prone hissa historically rahe hain (malformed/malicious packets se infinite loops ya crashes).
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek treasure hunt jahan har clue sirf PEHLE wale se KAM number wale room ki taraf point kar sakta hai -- kabhi bhi aage ya wahi room repeat nahi point kar sakta, isliye hunt zaroor khatam hoga (rooms finite hain aur number hamesha ghat raha hai), chahe kitni bhi clues follow karo (max 32 tak).
how_it_works: `if (target >= runStart) throw` backward-only rule; `if (++jumps > MAX_POINTER_JUMPS) throw` hard cap; `runStart = target` har jump ke baad update hota hai.
in_this_project: src/wire.ts readName(): `if (target >= runStart) throw new WireError(...)`; `if (++jumps > MAX_POINTER_JUMPS) throw new WireError(...)`; test cases '1-jump, 32-jump, 33-jump (rejected), self/forward pointer (rejected)' in README.md.
advantages: Guarantee termination without needing a visited-set or extra memory -- just one integer comparison
Two independent defenses (strictly-decreasing + hard cap) mean one alone failing still leaves protection
disadvantages: Strictly-backward rule rejects some theoretically-valid-but-unusual packets that point forward (not seen in practice, so low cost)
MAX_POINTER_JUMPS is a somewhat arbitrary constant (32) -- a legitimate deeply-nested name could theoretically need more, though none do in practice
common_mistakes: Sirf ek rule (jaise sirf jump count) implement karna aur backward-only check miss kar dena
runStart ko update na karna har jump ke baad, jisse multiple jumps ka protection todd jaata hai
follow_up_questions: Agar sirf MAX_POINTER_JUMPS hota, backward-only check na hota, kya exploit possible hota?
Agar sirf backward-only hota, MAX_POINTER_JUMPS na hota, kaunsa attack still possible hota?
Yeh approach 15-dns-resolver mein bhi same hai -- dono projects mein yeh idea kyun reuse hua?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Combining two independent defenses (strictly-decreasing target + hard jump cap) is defense-in-depth: either one alone would likely suffice for a well-formed-adversary, but keeping both costs almost nothing and protects against a bug in either check.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If the backward-only check were removed (and only the jump cap remained), a pointer could point forward into not-yet-decoded bytes, or at itself, and (depending on what's there) cause unpredictable reads or an effectively infinite loop within the 32-jump budget being gamed by chained forward jumps that never actually make progress toward termination in a bounded buffer.
advanced.alternatives: An alternative to strictly-decreasing targets is a visited-offsets Set, rejecting any already-visited offset -- correct but needs O(jumps) extra memory per name decode; the strictly-decreasing rule gets the same guarantee with O(1) extra state.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This check runs per answer-name decode; at 10x/100x query volume the cost is still O(1) per jump, so it scales linearly with traffic, not quadratically -- no special concern at higher scale.
advanced.production_improvements: None needed functionally; a production hardening would be to also cap total decode time per packet (a deeply pathological but technically-valid chain of max-length labels combined with jumps) as a defense against combined attacks, though this project's fixed caps already bound that tightly.

question: What did the mutation-testing gaps (WIRE5, TRANSPORT1, PROXY3) reveal about the difference between a test suite passing and a specific guard actually being exercised?
answer_hinglish:
Mutation testing mein ek specific line/check deliberately tod dete hain, poori suite chalate hain, aur dekhte hain kya koi test fail hota hai. '89 tests pass' sunke lagta hai sab guards verified hain, par teen cases mein yeh galat nikla.

WIRE5: reserved label-type (0x40/0x80) check hata dene par bhi tests PASS ho gaye, kyunki existing test buffer mein itne kam trailing bytes the ki ek ALAG, unrelated truncation/bounds check USSE PEHLE hi fail kar deta tha -- reserved-type check khud kabhi 'the one that caught it' nahi bana. Fix: ek naya test jisme 0x40 label ke baad 64 REAL valid-looking bytes hain -- ab koi bounds check fire nahi hoga, SIRF reserved-type check hi reject kar sakta hai.

TRANSPORT1: har test ka 'upstream' SIRF EK hi responder tha, isliye wrong-source-address check ke paas FILTER karne ko kuch tha hi nahi (koi second sender kabhi nahi tha). Fix: ek test-only `onUdpBound` hook add kiya jo humara apna ephemeral port reveal karta hai bind hone ke turant baad, taaki ek rogue socket ek spoofed reply bhej sake REAL upstream se PEHLE -- is tarah check genuinely EXERCISE hota hai.

PROXY3: stub upstream hamesha correct id/QR ke saath jawab deta tha, isliye id/QR verification check kabhi 'right vs wrong answer' ke beech khada nahi tha. Fix: ek naya `wrong-id` stub behavior jo `(id+1)` se jawab deta hai, plus test jo assert karta hai client ko apne hi ID ke saath SERVFAIL milta hai.

Teeno case common lesson: 'test suite ke paas hona' aur 'guard genuinely exercised hona' ALAG baatein hain -- ek check accidentally kisi UNRELATED check se overlap kar sakta hai aur phir bhi 'caught' dikhega.
why_needed: Yeh honest testing-methodology awareness dikhata hai -- senior engineers 'all tests pass' ko blindly trust nahi karte, woh verify karte hain ki HAR individual guard genuinely tested hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek fire alarm test mein alarm baj gaya, par pata chale ki asal mein smoke detector nahi, balki bagal wala heat sensor (jo alag wajah se tha) baja tha -- test 'pass' hua, par jo cheez test karni thi usne kuch kiya hi nahi.
how_it_works: Har mutation check: ek exact text replacement in src/, pura suite run, result record, file restore (verified byte-for-byte re-read), aage badho.
in_this_project: test/invariant.test.ts aur README.md ki mutation table; `onUdpBound` hook src/transport.ts ForwardOptions mein; `wrong-id` behavior src/stub-upstream.ts StubBehavior mein.
advantages: Mutation testing un gaps ko dhoondta hai jo code-coverage tools miss kar jaate hain (line 'covered' hoti hai, par guard genuinely tested nahi)
Har gap close karne se ek concrete, specific naya test bana jo future regressions ko bhi catch karega
disadvantages: Mutation testing manual/slow hai (har mutation ke baad poori suite run + file restore verify)
Sirf wahi mutations try kiye jaate hain jo socha gaya -- koi automated tool nahi tha jo saari possible mutations generate kare
common_mistakes: 'Test caught it' dekh kar maan lena ki specific check hi responsible thi, bina verify kiye ki KAUN sa assertion fail hua
Mutation testing ko ek-baar ka activity samajh lena, jab yeh refactoring ke baad bhi dobara karne layak hai
follow_up_questions: Ek check jo 'caught' dikh raha hai kisi UNRELATED reason se, aise case ko systematically kaise dhoondhte?
Kya coverage percentage (line/branch) yeh gaps dikha deta, ya mutation testing hi zaroori tha?
Production mein mutation testing ko CI mein regularly chalana chahiye, ya sirf occasional audit ke taur par?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Mutation testing trades extra engineering time (writing + running mutations manually) for a much stronger confidence signal than coverage alone; coverage tells you a line RAN, mutation testing tells you a line's ABSENCE would have been noticed.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without closing these gaps, a future refactor could silently remove the reserved-label-type check, the wrong-source defense, or the id/QR verification, and the existing 88/89-test suite would still show green -- a real correctness or security regression shipping unnoticed.
advanced.alternatives: An automated mutation-testing tool (like Stryker for JS/TS) could generate and run many more mutations automatically instead of this project's manual, hand-picked set -- more thorough but slower to run and sometimes noisier (equivalent mutants).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This is a development-time practice, not a runtime concern, so it does not change with query volume; at a larger codebase scale, manual mutation testing (as done here, one at a time with careful restore) would not scale well and an automated tool would become necessary.
advanced.production_improvements: Adding an automated mutation-testing tool to CI (even run less frequently than unit tests, e.g. nightly) would catch this class of gap automatically going forward instead of relying on a one-time manual audit.

question: Where does this proxy sit relative to a home router / DHCP setup if you wanted every device on the network to use it?
answer_hinglish:
Normally jab koi device (phone, laptop) network se join karta hai, DHCP server (zyadatar router) use IP address ke saath DNS server ka address bhi deta hai. Agar hum chahte hain ki PURA network (saare devices) is sinkhole proxy se guzre, toh do tareeke hain: (1) har device par manually DNS server address set karo (humari proxy ki IP), ya (2) router ki DHCP settings mein DNS server ka address badal do us proxy ki IP par -- isse HAR naya device automatically yeh use karega.

Isme ek practical catch hai: port 53 par bind karne ke liye admin/root privileges chahiye hoti hain, isliye yeh proxy by default high port 15353 par chalta hai (testing ke liye). Real deployment mein ise 53 par chalana padega (ya ek firewall/NAT rule se 53 -> 15353 redirect karna padega), aur `allowNonLoopback` explicitly set karna padega kyunki default loopback-only bind hai.

Yeh exact Pi-hole ka bhi deployment model hai -- ek chhoti machine (jaise Raspberry Pi) network mein kahin chalti hai, DHCP use point karta hai, aur SAARI devices ki DNS traffic usse guzarti hai bina har device par kuch manually configure kiye.
why_needed: System design interview mein 'yeh component real network mein kaise fit hota hai' ek common follow-up hota hai -- code se network topology tak connect karna important skill hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek building ka reception desk sabko bata de 'ab se sawaal yahan poochho' -- har naya aane wala automatically wahi poochhta hai, bina individually bataye.
how_it_works: DHCP server apne lease options mein DNS server IP deta hai; proxy us IP par UDP:53 (ya configured port) par sunta hai.
in_this_project: src/server.ts SinkholeServerOptions mein `port` (default 15353) aur `allowNonLoopback` flag -- yeh exactly woh knobs hain jo real-network deployment ke liye change karne padte.
advantages: Ek baar DHCP configure karne se poora network cover ho jaata hai, per-device setup nahi chahiye
Central jagah se blocking/caching policy enforce hoti hai
disadvantages: Proxy khud ek single point of failure ban jaata hai poore network ke DNS ke liye
Port 53 par bind karne ke liye elevated privileges chahiye, jo deployment ko thoda complex banata hai
common_mistakes: allowNonLoopback set na karna aur phir confuse hona ki proxy network devices se queries kyun nahi le raha
Soch lena ki per-device DNS setting DHCP se automatically override ho jaayegi
follow_up_questions: Agar proxy crash ho jaaye, poore network ka internet access kya affect hoga?
IPv6-only ya dual-stack network mein kya extra consideration hai?
Router ki DHCP settings badalna vs ek firewall redirect rule -- kaunsa approach better hai aur kyun?

question: How does this project conceptually compose with 15-dns-resolver in this repo -- could they work together?
answer_hinglish:
Dono projects wire format basics, TC-bit-to-TCP-retry pattern, aur stub-server-on-high-port test setup SHARE karte hain -- par unka JOB bilkul alag hai. 15-dns-resolver ek ITERATIVE RESOLVER hai: woh root se shuru karke, referrals follow karke, arbitrary authoritative servers se baat karke, ek naam resolve karta hai khud se. Yeh project (25-dns-sinkhole) ek PROXY hai: woh blocklist check karta hai aur baaki sab EK configured upstream ko forward karta hai -- khud resolve nahi karta.

Yeh dono composable hain CONCEPTUALLY: sinkhole proxy ka 'upstream' field kisi bhi DNS server ki tarah treat hota hai -- agar iske `upstream` ko 15-dns-resolver ke instance par point kar diya jaaye (agar woh ek network-listening server ki tarah expose ho), toh pura chain ban jaata: client -> sinkhole proxy (block/cache check) -> 15-dns-resolver (asli iterative resolution) -> internet ke authoritative servers.

Yeh dono projects CODE share nahi karte (25-dns-sinkhole ek fresh, self-contained implementation hai, 15-dns-resolver ke package par depend nahi karta) -- sirf IDEAS reuse hoti hain. Yeh ek deliberate choice hai: har project apne aap mein complete aur readable rehta hai, bina cross-project dependency management ke overhead ke.
why_needed: Multi-component system design mein 'kaunsa piece kis role mein hai, aur woh ek dusre ke saath kaise chain ho sakte hain' samajhna zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek building ka security gate (sinkhole proxy, kuch logon ko turant rok deta hai) aur andar ek poora navigation system (15-dns-resolver, jo har room tak ka raasta khud dhoondta hai) -- security gate navigation system ko call kar sakta hai jab zaroorat ho.
how_it_works: SinkholeProxyOptions.upstream ek generic Endpoint hai (host + port) -- yeh kisi bhi DNS-speaking server ko point kar sakta hai, chahe woh real 1.1.1.1 ho ya ek locally-running 15-dns-resolver instance.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts Endpoint interface aur SinkholeProxyOptions.upstream -- yahi generality compose-ability deti hai, bina kisi explicit 15-dns-resolver import ke.
advantages: Dono projects independently readable/testable hain, ek dusre par depend nahi karte
Chaining conceptually possible hai bina koi tight coupling ke, sirf network endpoint ke zariye
disadvantages: Koi shared code maintenance ka fayda nahi milta (jaise ek bug dono mein fix karna, alag-alag karna padega)
Agar dono ek saath chalayein, ek extra network hop (latency) add hota hai chain mein
common_mistakes: Sochna ki yeh dono projects package-level dependency share karte hain
Resolver aur proxy ke roles ko mix kar dena ek hi mental model mein
follow_up_questions: Agar chain banayein (sinkhole -> 15-dns-resolver), latency kaise measure/optimize karoge?
Kya dono projects ke beech code sharing (ek shared package) better hota, ya alag rehna sahi choice hai?
15-dns-resolver ka khud ka caching aur is proxy ka caching dono active hon toh double-caching ka kya effect hoga?

question: What would you need to add if you wanted a single sinkhole deployment to serve a whole office network across multiple machines?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi yeh ek single-process, single-machine design hai -- in-memory BlockList (trie) aur in-memory ResponseCache, dono ek hi process ke memory mein hain. Ek office network ke liye (sayad sirf EK machine par load badhane ke liye, ya high-availability ke liye MULTIPLE machines), kuch real changes chahenge:

(1) **High availability**: agar woh single machine down ho jaaye, poore office ka DNS ruk jaata hai. Fix: do ya zyada instances chalao, aur router/DHCP mein PRIMARY + SECONDARY DNS dono configure karo (yeh DNS protocol ka built-in failover hai, client khud secondary try karta hai agar primary timeout de).

(2) **Shared state across instances**: agar multiple instances hon, har ek ka apna ALAG in-memory cache hoga -- koi coordination nahi hai. Chhoti scale par yeh theek hai (har instance apna cache warm kar lega), par consistency guarantee nahi milti (ek instance pe fresh, dusre pe stale TTL dikh sakta).

(3) **Blocklist sync**: har instance ko same blocklist chahiye -- abhi yeh ek file se load hoti hai (loadBlockListFile), toh ek shared file/config-management process chahiye taaki saari instances consistent list use karein.

(4) **Capacity**: har forwarded query ek ephemeral socket leta hai (SINK-019) -- office-scale traffic par yeh fine hai, par bahut zyada concurrent clients par ephemeral port limits hit ho sakte.

Yeh sab 'Stage 2+' scope hai (PLAN.md mein explicitly 'not started' -- config hot-reload, multiple blocklists, stats page) -- is project ka Stage 1 single-machine, single-process use case tak hi scoped hai.
why_needed: Single-machine prototype ko multi-machine production deployment mein scale karna ek classic system-design question hai -- yeh dikhata hai candidate single-process assumptions ko identify kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek chhoti dukaan jo ek hi cashier se chalti hai -- office-scale banane ke liye sirf 'zyada cashiers' nahi, balki ek shared inventory system (blocklist sync) aur backup cashier (failover) bhi chahiye.
how_it_works: Protocol-level failover DNS mein built-in hai (client khud multiple configured DNS servers try karta hai); application-level sync (blocklist, cache) iss project mein implement nahi hai.
in_this_project: src/blocklist.ts loadBlockListFile() ek local file se ek-baar load hota hai process start par -- koi distributed sync mechanism nahi hai.
advantages: DNS protocol ka built-in primary/secondary failover simple HA deta hai bina application changes ke
Har instance independent hai -- ek crash dusre ko affect nahi karta
disadvantages: Cache coordination na hone se duplicate upstream calls ho sakte hain (ek hi naam, do instances, dono alag se fetch karte)
Blocklist sync manual/external process par depend karta hai, abhi yeh project khud nahi karta
common_mistakes: Sochna ki in-memory cache automatically distributed ho jaayega multiple instances mein
HA ko sirf 'ek aur machine add kar do' samajh lena bina blocklist consistency soche
follow_up_questions: Kya ek shared Redis cache yahan add karna sense banata, ya per-instance cache hi kaafi hai office scale par?
Blocklist ko kaise automatically sync karoge saari instances mein (push vs pull)?
Config hot-reload is missing feature ka HA ke saath kya connection hai?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: A shared cache (e.g. Redis) centralizes freshness but adds a network hop and a new dependency/failure mode; per-instance in-memory caches (current design) are simpler and faster but duplicate upstream calls across instances and can show inconsistent TTLs briefly.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If the single instance crashes with no secondary configured, the whole office loses DNS resolution immediately -- browsers, apps, everything that resolves names stops working, even though the rest of the network (routing, existing connections) is fine.
advanced.alternatives: A simpler HA approach than active-active instances is a hot-standby: one instance serves, a second is ready but idle, promoted manually or via a health check -- simpler coordination than shared caching, at the cost of some failover delay.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x the clients, a single instance's ephemeral-socket-per-query design (SINK-019) and loopback-bound default both need revisiting -- socket/port pressure and the need to bind non-loopback become real constraints, not edge cases.
advanced.production_improvements: Add primary/secondary via DHCP, a shared/central blocklist source (even just a periodically re-fetched file), and basic health-check-based alerting so a down instance is noticed before someone reports 'the internet is broken'.

question: Where exactly does caching sit in the request path, and what does that positioning buy (or cost) this design?
answer_hinglish:
Request path mein order yeh hai: (1) decode + validate, (2) BLOCKLIST check, (3) CACHE check, (4) forward upstream + cache store. Cache check blocklist check ke BAAD aata hai -- matlab blocked domains kabhi cache mein store/check nahi hoti, sirf allowed domains cache hoti hain.

Yeh positioning ek deliberate choice hai: blocklist check EK in-memory trie walk hai, bahut fast (no I/O), isliye use SABSE PEHLE karna hi sasta hai -- agar blocked hai, baaki sab (cache lookup, network) skip ho jaata hai, fastest possible path. Agar cache check PEHLE hoti, toh har blocked query bhi ek cache Map lookup 'waste' karti (chhoti cost hai, par bina fayde ke).

Cache khud forward-path aur response-path dono mein hai: forward se PEHLE check hoti hai (miss par hi network call lagti hai), aur successful forward ke BAAD store hoti hai. Yeh ek 'read-through cache' pattern hai -- proxy khud cache aur upstream ke beech ka coordinator hai, caller (client) ko cache ki existence ka pata hi nahi chalta.
why_needed: Request-path ordering ek chhoti par real performance/correctness decision hai -- interview mein 'kyun yeh order hai, ulta kyun nahi' pucha ja sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek restaurant mein pehle security check (ID proof, blocked list) hota hai, phir hi waiter order ke liye kitchen (cache/inventory) check karta hai -- blocked logon ke liye kitchen check karne ka koi fayda nahi.
how_it_works: handle() sequentially: blocklist check -> early return if blocked -> cache.get() -> early return if hit -> forwardQuery() -> cache.put() on success -> return reply.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts handle(): blocklist check block se cache.get() call PEHLE aata hai code mein, exact order jo yahan describe hua.
advantages: Blocked queries ka fastest-possible path hai, cache lookup bhi skip ho jaata hai
Cache sirf useful entries store karti hai (allowed domains), wasted space nahi
disadvantages: Agar ek domain blocklist se REMOVE ho jaaye runtime mein (abhi unsupported), uska cache kabhi nahi bana hota, pehli query hamesha upstream jaayegi
Read-through pattern matlab cache miss ka latency client ko directly dikhta hai (no background pre-warm)
common_mistakes: Cache check ko blocklist check se PEHLE rakh dena, jo chhota par avoidable overhead add karta
Yeh maan lena ki block response bhi kahin cache ho rahi hai (nahi hoti)
follow_up_questions: Kya block responses ko bhi cache karna chahiye, ya woh already itna fast hain ki zaroorat nahi?
Agar cache miss rate high ho jaaye, kaunsa metric pehle dikhega?
Read-through vs write-through caching ka yahan kya matlab hota?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Checking the cheap, in-memory blocklist before the cache (also in-memory, but a different data structure and purpose) keeps the fast path fastest for the most common 'skip everything' case; the alternative ordering would add negligible cost here but has no benefit, so this is a case where the 'obviously right' order and the 'actually fastest' order happen to coincide.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If the cache were checked before the blocklist, a flood of queries for a blocked domain would still do a cache Map lookup each time (a wasted, if cheap, operation) before being blocked -- not a real failure, but a measurable inefficiency under a block-domain-heavy query mix.
advanced.alternatives: A write-through design (populate cache proactively rather than only on first miss) would avoid the first-query latency hit but adds complexity (what to pre-populate, when) with no clear benefit for a reactive proxy that doesn't know in advance what clients will ask.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At high query volume, this ordering matters more: a large fraction of ad/tracker-heavy traffic in practice is REPEATED requests to a small set of blocked domains, so keeping the blocked path cheap (no map lookup, no network) is exactly the right optimization target at scale.
advanced.production_improvements: Expose cache hit-rate and blocked-rate as separate metrics (stats.cacheHits / stats.blocked / stats.total already exist in-memory) so this ordering's actual benefit can be measured against real traffic, not just reasoned about.

question: Why doesn't this proxy reproduce 15-dns-resolver's full Kaminsky-style spoofing defence against the upstream?
answer_hinglish:
15-dns-resolver ek iterative resolver hai -- woh arbitrary, never-before-talked-to authoritative servers se baat karta hai poore internet mein. Kisi bhi aise query ke liye, ek attacker (jo yeh janta hai ki humne kisi naam ke liye kisi server se poocha hai) ek FAKE reply bhejne ki koshish kar sakta hai, correct transaction ID guess karke (Kaminsky attack) -- isliye woh resolver har query ke liye RANDOM source port AND random transaction ID dono use karta hai, taaki guessing practically impossible ho.

Yeh proxy sirf EK configured, TRUSTED upstream se baat karta hai (jaise 1.1.1.1, bilkul Pi-hole jaise role mein).
